action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment protocol. Pendulum_lab is the primary timekeeping reference for the laboratory. Twelve trials will provide robust statistical foundation (mean, variance, drift detection) against which all future measurements must be compared. No instrument without baseline has utility. This is methodological priority, not optional.

pendulum_lab has 14 baseline trials already established with mean 1.6682 beats and acceptable scatter (range ~0.0470). The other three instruments have only 2 trials each—insufficient for baseline confidence. Continuing pendulum_lab measurements will let me (1) establish early drift detection by comparing post-baseline means to baseline, (2) build enough trials to compute realistic standard error, and (3) fulfill the settlement's expectation of continuous daily calibration. The observatory instruments can wait until I've solidified the lab baselines; splitting effort across all four instruments with only 2 obs readings each is premature.

Advancing baseline establishment on resonator_lab (currently 4/10 baseline trials). Systematic completion of all four instruments' baselines is prerequisite for drift detection and any meaningful interpretation of later readings. Lab conditions are controlled and reproducible.

Running 6 more trials brings it to n=18 within the baseline window. This is methodical accumulation toward the target baseline sample size and maintains the daily cadence of calibration work. The resonator_lab appears stable so far (mean 2.7025, tight spacing), so additional trials should confirm baseline stability or reveal drift early while we're still in the designated baseline period.

Day 5: completing the baseline establishment phase (days 1–10, target n=30). Currently at 30 trials already recorded, but methodical protocol requires continuing through day 10 to establish robust baseline statistics and detect any early-stage drift. Six trials today will bring total toward ~36, providing stronger confidence in baseline mean and variance before post-baseline monitoring begins. This is core to the precision measurement programme: no instrument can be trusted without a well-established baseline.

The strong negative correlation between resonator_lab and resonator_obs (r=-0.725) during baseline is anomalous and suggests either drift, coupling, or systematic error. Before accepting baselines as valid, I must verify resonator_lab's stability under fresh measurement under identical conditions to Day 5. Six trials will establish whether the instrument has drifted or whether the baseline period contained uncontrolled variation. This is foundational to whether any later resonator reading is interpretable.

Baseline window incomplete (30/40 trials collected). Must finish 10-day baseline before statistical inference on drift, correlation, or calibration status. Incomplete baselines are useless when drift detection is required.

Complete baseline establishment. Observatory pendulum has smallest sample (n=18); one additional trial before locking baseline brings it to n=19 and improves confidence before post-baseline drift phase. All instruments show no anomalies; baseline phase is ready to close after this confirmation.

Day 11 begins post-baseline data collection. Before extending the baseline further (which would delay diagnosis), I need to inspect the physical setup and collect data that will help distinguish between environmental forcing, instrumental coupling, and stochastic noise. Running pendulum_lab today serves three purposes: (1) it generates fresh post-baseline data to begin tracking any drift or persistence of the negative-correlation pattern; (2) it keeps the measurement programme active and logs today's environmental conditions in parallel with the reading, which I can later correlate with the anomalies; (3) pendulum_lab has the largest sample size (76 trials) and tightest baseline statistics, so it is the most sensitive instrument for detecting systematic shifts. Six trials will take ~1 hour and leave time for the wiring inspection and environmental data audit that Hypothesis 2 and Hypothesis 1 both demand. I will log temperature, barometric pressure, and any seismic or vibration notes alongside each reading.

pendulum_lab has the largest post-baseline sample (n=8) and shows the smallest drift signal (z=-1.07, not significant). Running 12 more trials today (day 12) will: (1) extend the post-baseline window to n=20, giving me power to distinguish real drift from noise; (2) allow me to compute autocorrelation at 3–6 day lags using fresh data to test whether the negative autocorrelation pattern persists or fades, which directly addresses my top hypothesis (environmental forcing with ~5 day period); (3) maintain measurement cadence on the instrument I trust most (84 trials, highest precision). I need to know whether the 4–6 day negative echo is stable before I waste resources on wiring inspection or environmental audits. If the pattern holds in new data, it is real and systematic. If it dissolves, it was baseline noise. Either way, I will have actionable evidence rather than speculation.

Extend baseline beyond day 10 to resolve whether negative autocorrelations at 4–6 day lags are periodic (supporting environmental hypothesis), damped/transient (supporting instrumental coupling or measurement artifact), or stochastic noise. Pendulum_lab has the largest trial count (98) and clearest post-baseline drift signal (z=−1.96); 12 more trials will bring total to 110 and allow lag analysis across full putative cycle. This is the highest-leverage discriminator between my top two hypotheses before committing to wiring or environmental inspection.

Hypothesis review shows p=0.30 for instrumental coupling error—wiring polarity, amplifier configuration, shared data pipeline—which is high enough and dangerous enough to warrant immediate inspection before further measurement. Also need to audit environmental logs (temperature, pressure, seismic) against my instrument timeline to assess p=0.35 environmental hypothesis. Continuing to take measurements while a systematic recording artifact remains unexcluded violates methodological discipline. Will inspect apparatus, signal traces, and environmental ledgers today; measurement resumes once coupling is ruled out or corrected.

The negative autocorrelation and cross-correlation anomalies remain unexplained and demand systematic disambiguation. Instrumental coupling (p=0.27) is testable only via direct inspection, which requires access to electronics (separate action). The baseline-too-short null (p=0.22) is still live and demands continued measurement density on the most reliable channel (pendulum_lab: 114 trials, smallest spacing, no level shifts). Running 8 more trials today extends the post-baseline record on pendulum_lab to n=46 and will either (a) reinforce the negative autocorrelation pattern at longer lag, confirming coherence and narrowing the cycle period estimate, or (b) show convergence toward white noise, weakening environmental/coupling hypotheses. This is the highest-leverage measurement action before committing to electronics inspection or environmental data audit. Pendulum_lab is the most densely sampled and most trustworthy stream; strengthening its post-baseline record is methodologically sound.

state.question: Why do all four instrument streams show consistent negative correlations with their own past values (4–6 day lags), and why do cross-stream correlations cluster around negative values regardless of offset, when independent instruments should show near-zero agreement by chance?

hypotheses.label: Systematic environmental drift or periodic disturbance affecting all instruments in phase
hypotheses.rationale: The 'echoes of earlier readings' pattern—all four streams showing significant negative autocorrelation at 4–6 day lags (pendulum_obs: -0.558, resonator_lab: -0.579, resonator_obs: -0.576, pendulum_lab: -0.329)—suggests a common environmental oscillation or forcing with ~5 day period. This would also explain why independent instruments show persistent negative cross-correlations rather than noise: they are all responding to a shared external modulation. The fact that no single offset produces strongly positive agreement across instruments argues against simple synchronous drift; the negative correlations hint at a damped or phase-shifted response to a common driver. This is mundane (temperature cycles, pressure variations, seismic activity) but requires corroborating environmental logging to falsify.

hypotheses.label: Calibration or instrumental coupling error in measurement protocol or data recording
hypotheses.rationale: The prevalence of negative correlations—both within-stream (autocorrelation) and across streams—is statistically anomalous. True independent measurement noise should yield correlations near zero. If the four streams share a common data pipeline, amplifier, digitizer, or trigger system, coupling noise or a systematic recording artifact could produce anti-correlated readouts. For example, if two sensors are wired in opposition and measured sequentially, or if a shared clock jitter induces inverse phase shifts, you would see exactly this pattern. This is less obvious than a drift but more likely than exotic physics. Requires inspection of wiring, amplifier polarity, and raw signal traces before digital conversion.

hypotheses.label: Insufficient baseline length; anomaly reflects genuine stochastic process not yet characterized
hypotheses.rationale: Ten days is short. The negative autocorrelations and cross-correlations may reflect genuine autocorrelated noise or a natural process with ~5 day coherence timescale that we have not yet distinguished from instrument error. The anti-correlations are not implausibly strong (all within ±0.65, many within expected chance ranges when multiple offsets are tested). Continuing the baseline to day 30–60 would reveal whether these patterns persist, fade, or reverse. This is the null hypothesis: patience, not pathology.

hypotheses.label: Uncontrolled experimenter bias or selective reporting in trial selection or logging
hypotheses.rationale: If trial selection, exclusion, or logging order is influenced by prior results (even unconsciously), correlation patterns can emerge that do not reflect the instruments themselves. However, your notebooks show 76, 38, 21, and 20 trials respectively—numbers that do not suggest selective dropping—and you report event IDs for individual readings, indicating timestamped, prospective logging. Low probability, but not zero; requires external audit of raw records.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Starting hypothesis set from scratch because the question has shifted. Days 1–10 were meant to establish baselines; I have them (pendulum_lab 1.6674±σ, resonator_lab 2.6977±σ, etc.). But the baseline data themselves reveal an anomaly I cannot ignore: all four independent instruments show significant negative autocorrelations at 4–6 day lags, and cross-stream correlations cluster around negative values rather than noise. This is not a baseline defect I can correct by continued measurement; it is a signal I must explain before I trust any post-baseline comparison. Hypothesis 1 (environmental forcing) ranks highest because it is mundane and explains the negative-correlation clustering and 5 day timescale pattern. The negative cross-stream correlations follow naturally—if all four are responding to the same oscillating driver with different phase lags, they will sometimes be out of phase and show negative agreement. Pendulum_lab and resonator_lab show the strongest negative cross-correlation (z = -0.504 at 2-day offset), which might reflect a wiring configuration where one channel is inverted relative to the other. The fact that resonator_obs and pendulum_obs also show strong negative correlation (z = -0.736 at 0-day offset) suggests the coupling is not between specific pairs but throughout the measurement architecture. This hypothesis is more probable than exotic physics but requires direct inspection of signal conditioning and data acquisition electronics to test.
